idiom_name: guard class with a private resource + IPrincipal/ClaimsPrincipal policy check; DispatchProxy for transparent guards
implementation_notes: The guard is hand-written (private field, public methods that consult the policy before touching the resource) and the language gives it only compile-time accessibility: 'private: Only code declared in the same class or struct can access this member', 'internal: Only code in the same assembly can access this type or member' - the assembly is a packaging boundary, and reflection can reach non-public members. What the framework supplies is the policy side of the pattern: IPrincipal/ClaimsPrincipal represents 'the security context of the user on whose behalf the code is running, including that user's identity (IIdentity) and any roles to which they belong', and IsInRole is the role check the guard calls. The runtime sandbox that once accompanied this is gone: 'CAS is not supported in .NET Core, .NET 5, or later versions. CAS is not supported by versions of C# later than 7.0', and the archived guidance already said CAS should not be used to enforce security boundaries. A method-level transparent guard can be generated instead of written: System.Reflection.DispatchProxy 'provides a mechanism for instantiating proxy objects and handling their method dispatch', with Invoke called on every generated-proxy call - the library realization of the protection proxy.
pitfalls: Code Access Security is gone: 'CAS is not supported in .NET Core, .NET 5, or later versions', so a permission-demand sandbox cannot be rebuilt from the legacy System.Security.Permissions types - use OS/process isolation or the request pipeline instead.

Reflection and serialization reach private state (non-public binding in System.Reflection, formatters that set private fields), so private fields organize ownership but do not confine code running in the same process.

Do not confuse authentication with authorization: IPrincipal carries the identity, but the guard must evaluate a policy for the specific operation; IsInRole inline in twenty methods is exactly the drift this pattern removes.

A DI container hands out whatever is registered: if the resource (connection, HttpClient, client instance) is also registered and injected elsewhere, the guard is advisory - register only the guard and keep the resource's constructor internal.

variants.name: DispatchProxy-generated transparent guard
variants.implementation_notes: Where callers must keep using the resource's interface, .NET can generate the forwarding guard instead of having it written by hand: DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() 'creates an object instance that derives from class TProxy and implements interface T', and Invoke is called 'whenever any method on the generated proxy type is called', so the policy decision sits in one method for the whole surface. The real resource stays in the proxy's own state and is never exposed; the cost is that the guard's checks are centralized in Invoke (per-method rules keyed by MethodInfo) and that the proxy is a runtime-generated type, which reflection-heavy code can often see through. Prefer it when the interface is wide and the policy is uniform; prefer the hand-written class when the guard's surface should be narrower than the resource's.
pitfalls: Invoke sees method names/metadata, not intent: key policies on the method and its arguments explicitly, or a new interface method silently inherits another operation's permission.
The proxy type is generated at runtime and dispatch goes through reflection - hot paths pay for it, and Native AOT/trimming needs the proxy pattern to be declared or it may fail at runtime.
State lives on the proxy instance: a proxy cached or shared across requests crosses principals unless the policy is resolved from the current context rather than from captured state.
